articles.text: On January 17, Piedmont City Council voted to discontinue remote participation for most Commission and all Committee meetings as of March 1. Community members will still be able to comment remotely via Zoom for City Council and Planning Commission meetings. Park Commission and Recreation Commission meetings will continue to be broadcast live on KCOM and streamed on the city website. This format change was prompted by changes to state regulations governing public meetings, which had been relaxed at the beginning of the pandemic to support remote participation for members of legislative bodies. On October 17, 2022, Governor Newsom announced his intention to rescind the COVID- 19 State of Emergency at the end of this month, at which point members of City Councils, Boards, Commissions, and Committees statewide will be required to attend meetings in person, with limited exceptions. At the January 17 council meeting, city staff briefed council members on changes to teleconference regulations and asked the Council to give direction on whether to continue providing remote participation options for community members, After a detailed discussion, the Council chose to continue offering public comment remotely over Zoom for City Council and Planning Commission meetings only, due to low remote participation for other bodies and the strain on staff resources required to support hybrid meetings. Each remote or hybrid meeting requires an additional staff member, working overtime, to manage the logistics and operations of the virtual meeting. More information is available in the staff report for the January 17 City Council meeting, which can be found at bit.ly/3Ywsun8. For questions about remote participation in city government meetings, contact Communications Program Manager Echa Schneider by phone at 420-3039, or by email at eschneider@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Editor: Earlier this year, Piedmont Recreation Department announced a plan to eliminate tennis at the Linda Beach tennis courts, proceeding with a pickleball-only trial in an effort to assess the need for dedicated pickleball courts and a potential goal of establishing it at these courts. However, the current trial design has inherent bias and may be unjustified. Over the past five years, pickleball has gained free access to 4-6 courts seven days per week, the same number as Alameda whose population is eight times that of Piedmont. So how many players on our courts are also tax-paying residents of Piedmont? This question can be answered implementing the same resident-only decal system used for tennis, creating revenue to maintain the courts. With this equitable and accessible solution, PRD can quantify Piedmont residents’ needs, monitor for growth within our community and appropriately allocate resources. articles.text: At a Planning Commission meeting on February 13, Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald and Planning Department Director Kevin Jackson provided the Commission with an update on the status of Piedmont’s 6th Cycle Housing Element. The Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 — a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. This Element drafting cycle is repeated every eight years. On November 15, 2022, said MacDonald, “City Council authorized staff to file the Element with the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).” This began the 90-day period which HCD has to review the Element and give comments. Jackson confirmed that “the HCD is concluding its review this week.” The state also requires, through the California Environmental Quality Act, that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. On December 9, 2022, the city published an Initial Study-Negative Declaration determining that the Housing Element would not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. On January 12 the Planning Commission recommended during a public hearing that City Council adopt the Element. On January 17 the council unanimously voted to issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Plan, which is a major part of the Element, aims to improve existing facilities and incorporate 132 units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, along Moraga Avenue; 60 units of this housing would be available to lower-income households. The land affected by the Moraga Canyon Plan includes Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. MacDonald said that the RFP, which outlines the requirements for a consultant’s analysis of this plan, was issued on January 23. On February 8, “city staff held a pre-bid conference call for prospective proposers. Approximately 11 firms participated in the conference call.” Throughout the process of drafting the Specific Plan and the Housing Element, said Jackson, “the city’s hosted dozens of public engagement events, workshops, surveys, online tools, open houses and town halls, and over 1000 Piedmonters participated in the planning process. We received over 550 comments from residents, school district and city employees, property owners, business leaders, religious leaders and other members of the community. I can’t think of any other city that has been able to engage this a large percentage of its population around the topic of housing.” He said that the comments the city expects to receive from HCD “will probably be mostly technical comments that we can solve fairly quickly,” given that city staff have already met several times with HCD staff, even giving the state reviewer a tour — which Jackson led — of Piedmont Housing Element sites on January 13. After the city does receive comments this week and amend the Element to comply with them, he expects to bring the Housing Element to City Council for adoption in late February or March. “I just want to say that I’m appreciative of the community’s response to the challenges of planning for 587 new housing units,” said Jackson. “I’m proud to say that community members have responded to the state’s call to welcome more people of all backgrounds to live in Piedmont.” More information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the Housing Element process, contact Kevin Jackson by email kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.

articles.text: Part 3 in a series Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Tax-Aid Tax-Aid, based in San Francisco, offers free remote and in-person tax help from expert Bay Area tax volunteers. The company’s large team of tax professional volunteers handle households earning less than $60,000 a year and offer free help in a client’s preferred language. Although volunteers are particularly needed ahead of this year’s tax season, there are plenty of opportunities after tax season ends as well. Visit tax-aid.org/tax-volunteers to sign up. The organization also accepts donations at tax-aid.org/donate-or-sponsor. East Bay SPCA The East Bay’s oldest animal welfare organization is always in need of volunteers. Volunteering is a wonderful way to improve the lives of animals in the shelter, and a variety of opportunities are available for all ages. East Bay SPCA’s Humane Education programs are particularly tailored for youth volunteers. Some examples of potential service projects include making dog treats, assisting with shelter laundry, socializing with animals in the SPCA’s care, and more. Participants will learn about responsible pet care, the medical needs of animals, and pet behavior. Other Oakland volunteer opportunities for adults and youth include feline or canine animal care, customer service, shelter care, pet food pantry distribution, event assistance, and animal training class assistance. Visit eastbayspca.org/get-involved/ volunteer/become-a-volunteer to sign up and learn more. Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) Students who have a love of art and are interested in the education field would enjoy volunteering at the Museum of Children’s Art (MOCHA) in Oakland. Tasks include everything from preparing art materials, to aiding youth art workshops and afterschool library events, to assisting with special events at the museum. Email info@ mocha.org for volunteer inquiries. Visit mocha.org to learn more about the museum. Project Open Hand Project Open Hand’s mission is to improve health outcomes by providing nutritious meals to the sick and vulnerable in the East Bay. Founded in 1985, the organization provides meals with love to critically ill neighbors and seniors. Each day, volunteers prepare 2,500 nutritious meals and provide 200 bags of healthy groceries. If you are interested in scheduling a weekly volunteer shift, Project Open Hand asks for a 6-month commitment, or 40 hours a semester for students. Contact volunteer@openhand.org with questions or to sign up, and visit openhand.org/volunteer/individual-volunteer to learn more about weekly kitchen, grocery center, meal site, and delivery volunteer opportunities. articles.text: Since March 19, 2018, when City Council adopted Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, the city has aimed to reduce GHG emissions 40% by 2030 and be on track to reduce emissions 80% by 2050. A crucial part of this plan is the electrification of homes, buildings, cars, and appliances. On February 13, city Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman spoke with the Piedmont Post about common electrification concerns regarding PG&E power outages and even rate hikes. “As PG&E continues to raise rates,” said Dykman, “I think that cost is always going to be a concern for those considering going electric. However, when you look at the forecast of where electricity rates and natural gas rates are heading, you see a far greater increase in natural gas rates, and a greater proportion [of this increase] going toward maintaining gas infrastructure and service lines.” Gas usage itself remains an issue in light of recent storms and cold spells; PG&E customers have used more natural gas this winter than the five-year historic average, with November usage 20% higher, December 10% higher, and January 10% higher. Despite this, the main concern is the skyrocketing price of these utilities. As of January 2023, the national average of combined utility bills was $328 a month. In the Oakland area, combined utility bills cost households an average of $564 a month. PG&E rates have increased faster than inflation for a decade, with residential rates rising 31% between 2009 and 2019, compared to the consumer price index of 19%. “As of January 25, PG&E projects that [residential energy bills] will be 32% higher from November 2022 through March 2023, compared to the same months last year” said Dykman. Despite these costs, the fact that PG&E shuts off power during periods of high demand and peak fire season is a deterrent to many who consider going electric. Last summer, state regulators fined the company $12 million over poor execution of the widespread power shutoffs that were meant to prevent wildfires in 2020. “To those worried about electric outages, I’d say that their circumstances would be closer [using natural gas] than they think. Many natural gas appliances also have fans, motors, or other ignitions requiring electricity to run. It’s very true that some essential appliances — like stoves — can be lit with matches if using natural gas, but it’s also important to remember that gas can also be cut off during emergencies.” How, then, would Piedmont support residents who have gone Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: On Monday, February 6 around 4 a.m., a 7.8 magnitude earthquake hit Turkey and Syria. The quake was the most powerful in the country since December 1939, when an earthquake killed 30,000 people in December 1939. As of Tuesday afternoon, February 14, the death toll passed 40,000. The epicenter was 14.2 miles north of Nurdaği, a city in Gaziantep province, where southeastern Turkey borders northwestern Syria. Aftershocks ripped throughout the day and region; the strongest one measured a magnitude of 7.5, 9 hours after and 59 miles north of the original epicenter. Tremors were felt as far away as Israel and Lebanon. Turkish President Recep Erdoğan declared a three-month state of emergency in 10 provinces affected by the earthquake. Turkey reported at least 5,434 deaths and 31,777 injuries. In government-controlled parts of Syria, at least 812 people were killed and 1,449 injured. Civil defense workers in the rebel-held northwest — which already faced a humanitarian crisis nearly 12 years into a bloody civil war — reported at least 1,020 deaths and 2,400 injuries. Thousands of buildings were flattened, leaving inhabitants homeless in near-freezing weather. Governments worldwide are pledging assistance and deploying aid as thousands of rescue workers desperately dig possible survivors from the rubble. The United States announced on Monday that it would deploy two specialized search-and-rescue teams of about 80 members each, one from Los Angeles and another from Virginia. Here are organizations working on rescue and recovery efforts. Donations are greatly needed. UNICEF The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund is in Syria and prioritizing water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition, and focusing on helping unaccompanied children locate their families. UNICEF is accepting donations at unicefusa.org. Global Giving Global Giving, which helps local nonprofit agencies, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3DSf8JI to help fund emergency medical workers’ ability to provide food, shelter and medicine, among other necessities. As needs in Turkey and Syria change, the organization will focus on longterm assistance. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies The IFRC is requesting donations for its Disaster Response Emergency Fund at bit.ly/3HFJe49 so it can send “immediate cash assistance.” OXFAM OXFAM, an international organization that fights poverty, is working with women’s cooperatives in Turkey to determine an appropriate immediate and longterm response plan. It is accepting donations at bit.ly/3YfjYso. CARE CARE, an organization that works with impoverished communities, is accepting donations that will go toward food, shelter and hygiene kits, among other items. Donate and learn more at bit.ly/3DRU3yO. Doctors Without Borders DWB, which responds to medical emergencies around the world, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3I7Jw5c. The Syrian American Medical Society SAMS is a United Statesbased humanitarian group that supplies medical care in Syria and nearby countries. At least one of its hospitals in northwestern Syria, Al Dana, received major damage. SAMS is collecting donations at bit.ly/3RJdBLz to deliver emergency aid. Save the Children Save the Children is accepting donations at bit.ly/3I6QmIb for its Children’s Emergency Fund, which will help provide children with food, shelter and warm clothing. The Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations UOSSM, which since 2012 has provided medical relief and health care services ins Syria and to Syrian refugees in Turkey, is collecting money at uossm.org/ donate. Empowering the TurkishAmerican Community ETAC, a nonprofit which provides support services and guidance to members of the Turkish community with lack of means or language skills, is collecting donations which will be sent directly and entirely to rescue teams. articles.text: Siddharth Bhatia, a junior at Piedmont High School, has been named winner of the Congressional App Challenge for the 13th Congressional District for an app he developed called “Pocket Congress.” The app provides easy access to a wealth of information about members of U.S. Congress, their background, congressional voting records, and how to get in touch with them. Bhatia was the sole winner in the District represented by Barbara Lee that includes Oakland, Piedmont, Berkeley, Emeryville, Albany, Alameda, and San Leandro. According to the congressional website, “The Congressional App Challenge is the most prestigious prize in student computer science.” Bhatia’s inspiration to create the app came while learning about government in a high school history class. ”They say that we are supposed to keep the representatives accountable. We elect them and they derive their power from us, but I feel there is this divide between us and our representatives,” said Bhatia. “After the TV ads and election in November they kind of disappear. How do said his dad, Rajeev Bhatia. Bhatia built Pocket Congress with the vision of increasing transparency through ease of access by the public. “What I’m most proud of is the app is just as easy as checking text messages. Anyone can now find out what their representative is doing,” he said. Pocket Congress utilizes information from the news organization Propublica that has huge data sets of congressional information. Propublica, is an independent New York-based, non-profit newsroom that produces investigative journalism, with updates three or four times a day. That information is now automatically synched with Bhatia’s app, making sure Pocket Congress is always evolving and up to date. “I just took all that data, formatted it and cleaned it up a little. I had no experience in coding before this, and I think this app goes to show how much you really can do on your own even if you don’t have the education or prior experience. Pocket Congress is fully functioning and free to download from the Apple App Store or by clicking Apps.apple.com/us/app/ pocket-congress/id6444019265. articles.text: Directly benefiting from its commitment to provide a safe and inclusive educational environment for all students and staff, Piedmont School District will receive a 3-year $200,000 grant as part of the California Department of Education’s Antibias Education Grant. With $20 million to eradicate racism in all California schools, the state has invited school districts to apply for an Antibias Education Grant. articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop One decided to take a trip back in time and explore the former immigration station at Angel Island, now a museum. After taking a short ferry ride to the island on February 11, the Scouts hiked up to the barracks where the immigrants – largely Chinese – were held. We were led on a guided tour through the building. It was heartbreaking to read famous poems on the walls, and to see the cramped living conditions. Immigrants were forced to endure these prison-like conditions for a few months while they were endlessly interrogated, in order to gain access to America. It operated from 1910 to 1940. The beautiful poetry that was carved into the walls was covered up with wood putty and lead paint by the government. Speaking of the government, they were pure devils. The walls were painted jade because of the stereotypical belief that all the Chinese are jade and chop suey. In the beginning, Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill enjoys the ferry ride with Troop One Scouts. Original beds at Angel Island immigration station Scouts pass the time waiting for their ferry by observing marine life in San Francisco Bay. there were no mattresses because the Chinese sleep on boards on the floor, right? The lights were bare bulbs and the beds were around 18 inches wide, stacked three tall, crammed together with no space or ladders between them. You know how you hate sharing a bathroom? Imagine sharing two bathrooms with 700. What happened at Angel Island was repulsive, patronizing, and should never, ever be repeated. However, by learning about Angel Island, and supporting each other, we can help prevent these dreadful events from repeating. The Scouts found comfort with a quick, uplifting hike to the nearby beach with breathtaking views of San Francisco Bay. The clouds and rain that had greeted us when we arrived had vanished, leaving a baking sun. It felt like the perfect metaphor for the trip: even when things are ugly or miserable, they can aways lift and be better. articles.text: Final interviews for a permanent Superintendent of Schools in Piedmont were concluded on Friday and Saturday, February 10 and 11, by the five members of the school board. Following the interviews, the job was offered to a candidate, who has accepted. The board is currently engaged in contract negotiations but has stated it won’t announce the name and details of the new superintendent until the March 8 school board meeting. The search firm, Leadership Associates, confirmed it received 39 requests for applications and applications from 22 candidates. The school board settled on interviewing six candidates in the first round on Friday, February 10. At that time each candidate received an one hour interview and responded to a set of 11 questions. “Questions covered a wide range of topics including: budget, board relations, labor negotiations, equity and belonging, educator hiring and retention, communications, and stakeholder engagement,” according to the Piedmont School Board. Three finalists were invited back for a second interview at a breakfast meeting on Saturday, February 11. The second interviews “were in-depth conversations that lasted 45 minutes,” stated the Piedmont School Board. The last time Piedmont hired a permanent Superintendent was eight years ago, a process that resulted in the hiring of Randy Booker. Eric Andrew, a Leadership Associates Consultant who helped lead Piedmont’s search this year, said he was pleased with the quantity and quality of applicants. Andrew explained that the job market has changed since 2015, especially since the pandemic and because of changes in policy and philosophy by school boards. Andrew, a former superintendent, has seen a trend for superintendents to have shorter tenures and retire earlier than in prior times. “Typically the retiring age for superintendents is 61 years of age after 30 years of service. Now, we are starting to see superintendents leave between age 55 and 58,” he said. “In some cases the pandemic took its toll, with masking debates, school reopenings, and some of the cultural wars in-terms of is the district going to implement equity, how far do you take it, how involved is it?” Andrew said. The regularly scheduled board meeting at which the new superintendent will be introduced is scheduled for 7:00 p.m. at City Hall on Wednesday, March 8.

articles.text: As we grow up, our dreams evolve and allow us to imagine the endless possibilities of where we can go and who we can become. In September 1992, Dr. Mae C. Jemison made history as the first Black woman to travel into space. Born in 1956 in Alabama, she grew up imagining that one day she would make it into space. As a child, she watched the original Star Trek shows, which inspired her to go into space. In an interview with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists & Engineers, Dr. Jemison discusses how the character of Nyota Uhura helped connect her idea of space travel by seeing Uhura in the role as a lieutenant in the show. Nichelle Nichols portrayed Lieutenant Uhura, also noteworthy because she was a Black woman playing an integral role on television. With her drive to reach the stars, Dr. Jemison’s journey began as she attended Stanford University where she received a Bachelor degree in Chemical Engineering and a Bachelor of Arts degree in African American Studies. She then gained a Doctorate in Medicine at Cornell Medical School. Now a physician, Dr. Jemison practiced medicine and joined the Peace Corps. In 1985, she applied to NASA’s astronaut program. According to the National Women’s History Museum, Dr. Dr. Mae C. Jemison was the first Black woman to travel into space. Jemison reapplied in 1987 due to NASA pausing acceptances because of the tragedy of the space shuttle Challenger. However, success came when Dr. Jemison was chosen to be a part of the STS-47 crew as a mission specialist. On September 12, 1992, Dr. Jemison and her crew were launched into space. Chabot Space & Science Center is home to the NASA Ames Visitor Center, which showcases Dr. Jemison’s Autogenic Feedback Training Exercise Suit (AFTE) and a signed replica flight suit. The AFTE suit was used to help astronauts adapt to the environment in space and then to readapt to the environment on Earth upon their return. Dr. Jemison was with NASA for six years. While talking with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists and Engineers, Dr. Jemison mentions a full-circle moment she experienced. Star Trek was an inspiration early on in her life and she later became a real-life star on the show. Dr. Jemison is a doctor, engineer, astronaut, and pioneer in the history of women in space. Before her time with NASA, she worked in a Cambodian refugee camp and went with a study group to Cuba. After her time with NASA, she continued her efforts and founded the nonprofit Dorothy Jemison Foundation for Excellence. She also developed an international space camp called The Earth We Share, and founded her own consulting company that focuses on science, technology, and social change. Dr. Jemison is an inspiration

articles.text: Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George in the backyard of their Wildwood Avenue home. Piedmont residents Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George found love in a law school class almost 45 years ago which continues to resonate today. Greg and Carolyn are both lawyers, both enjoy gardening and growing vegetables (think Harvest Festival). Even though he is Piedmont’s Mr. Jazz as the founder and longtime organizer of the annual Piedmont Jazz Festival, it was Carolyn who sparked his love of jazz. “Our law professor credited himself entirely with our happy relationship, because we had Remedies Class together,” she said with a smile. “He would always say ‘Ms. George, how would you respond to what Mr. Slatoff said about that?’ So he got us talking in class and then invited us to dinner a few times.” “Valentine’s Day has always been special,” said Greg. “The nice thing about it is that it’s kind of a moveable feast,” said Greg. “When we were first dating, we had absolutely nothing. We would have a bottle of Franzia champagne and couple of baubles and it was great.” To celebrate their sixth anniversary of dating the couple went to the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite, but Carolyn found that Greg was acting very weird. “He was not communicative and getting dressed in the closet; he was being skittish and I thought, well, that’s it. I’m so frustrated with him; he just can’t even talk anymore,” she said. The next morning Carolyn confronted her boyfriend, asking for an explanation. Greg replied, “Well, last night I had it all planned out. I was going to take you out for a walk in the moonlight and I would ask you to marry me.” Carolyn replied, with “Well, it was about 30 degrees below and there were wolves, why don’t you ask me now?” But Greg stayed with his idea. “I had a tuxedo and a great plan,” he recalled. Finally, Carolyn said, “Just ask me now!” Greg got on one knee and as she nodded yes, an eruption of applause and cheers was heard. Guests at the Ahwahnee behind a glass window had been watching the dynamic unfold and helped celebrate their union. Two weeks later they got married in a small ceremony, at the Unitarian Church on Van Ness in San Francisco. Due to the popularity of the dystopian book and film 1984, they felt the world was on the precipice of change so they decided to get married before 1984 ended – December 31. “It was $100 for the minister and $100 for the church if we had less than 10 people. So some of our family members had to act as photographers so we wouldn’t go over 10,” they said, taking turns narrating the story. Carolyn convinced her dad to use the money they would have spent on an expensive wedding to use as a down payment on a house. They lived in San Francisco for five years, then bought a house right on the Piedmont-Oakland border. After another six years they moved to Wildwood Avenue where their daughters Alexandra and Lara were born in 1990 and 1994. Through their leadership of the Piedmont Jazz Festival and Piedmont Harvest Festival the couple intertwines their interest as they have grown together. Carolyn chooses the judges for the Harvest Festival every year, and Greg not only runs the Jazz Festival, but creates the artwork every year for the flier. Both have been active members of St. John’s Episcopal Church in Montclair for many years. Their home represents their talents, Greg’s instruments (he is now in a stringed instrument phase) are all around the house, and his paintings adorn the walls. Their large backyard was used for subsistence farming by the previous owners. While on a somewhat smaller scale, their garden space is one of the major producers of fresh vegetables and fruits for the Edible Foot Contest at the Harvest Festival. Carolyn and Greg, have different views on what makes their bond so strong. “I think we’ve continued to be friends; it’s very important. I think we really, honestly enjoy each other’s company, and have built a life here that is all our life – not his life and my life,” Carolyn explained. “I think guys approach it differently,” he responded. “You don’t marry your best friend. For me, it was love at first sight; I was just smitten and that hasn’t changed,” Greg said.

articles.text: Bob and Kay Cheatham met at Murray High School in St. Paul, Minnesota 67 years ago. Kay, an extroverted cheerleader, made a plan in January of her Senior year of high school to ask Bob to the Senior Prom. It seems that the rest is history. Months ahead of the Prom, she already had her eyes set on him. “I made a calendar. I had to find him somewhere in the school in the halls of school or the lunchroom or somewhere and I had to say something to him. I did that, and the next day I resolved to say more that hi,” she recalled. Two days later, Kay and Bob ran into each other in the hallway, and eventually Bob offered to drive her home after a school basketball game. They stayed in touch through college, but it wasn’t until graduate school, when, separated by the Pacific Ocean, Kay made her final move. While teaching as a graduate student in Japan, Kay placed a long distance call to Bob to ask if she could visit him in Alaska during her spring break. At the time, Bob was a civil engineer and was a little reluctant to have Kay fly out. He was building his own house, which wasn’t yet complete. “I said ‘I’m flying out to visit you in Alaska’,” recalled Kay with a smile, “and he said ‘don’t come.’ So then I said. ‘will you see me if I come? And he said yes.” After one week of skiing and traveling, Bob proposed marriage in a restaurant on a little island outside Juneau, No surprise, Kay said yes. After their wedding in Minnesota in 1964, they took another spring break opportunity. This time it was Bob’s break from law school in order to have a honeymoon, with a destination unknown. “We didn’t know what the Ozarks were, but we decided we would go to the Ozarks,” said Kay. “The design of the trip, since I had five days for spring break, was to drive south for two and half days, stay somewhere and drive back,” said Bob. “We would stop at a gas staBob and Kay Cheatham in their backyard. tion and ask, ‘How far are the Ozarks?” started Kay. “Nobody really knew for sure. We’d ask, ‘Are we in the Ozarks now’?” Bob said finishing Kay’s sentence. Although they never found the Ozarks, Bob returned on time for the next semester and eventually became a lawyer and Kay a school psychologist. Kay and Bob would take many more trips together, including back to Japan where Kay had already made friends. While there, they lived in in a tea house in the backyard of a friend she met on a TV set while playing the role of an American mother in a program about Thanksgiving. Back in the states, Kay gave birth to their first child, Anne in Oakland. Lynn came two years later and their third child, Paul, was born in 1978, 10 years later. All three went to Piedmont school and now Kay and Bob have three granddaughters in Berkeley and three grandsons in Sebastopol. What’s the secret to their longevity? They never stopped dancing and were happy to talk about dancing last weekend in Rossmoor. “Bob’s secret is he is a really good dancer, I was interested in really learning the tango or Waltz, but Bob doesn’t like anyone to tell him how to dance,” Kay said with a grin. “We did take a lesson once, I think, upon your request.” Bob then reminded his wife. Although in their 80s the Cheathams remain remarkably active. “I can still bike. I’m walking with a cane because I can’t walk right, but I can bike just fine,” said Kay. With six decades of marriage and a smiling wife as credentials, Bob offered the following advice on staying together all these years. “Psychologically, when we get upset at the other person, it’s often a projection,” he said. When asked how to handle a situation when your partner appears to be projecting, Bob said, “The best thing would be to just listen and say nothing. I’m just beginning to learn that,” he said with a smile. The Cheathams observe Valentine’s Day every year. This Valentine’s Day Kay will be making her traditional heart-shaped brownies with red frosting to share with Bob, family in Berkeley and friends in Piedmont. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Plan for their future and yours. articles.text: When Dick and Mary Carter got married, it was the first day of 1984, a blistering hot Sunday in Washington, D.C., and the Washington Redskins were playing the Los Angeles Rams. “The priest kept interrupting the ceremony to give updates to people wondering about the score,” Dick said. “The Redskins went on to lose the Super Bowl, so it was a good day for a Mass.” Although Mary’s family lived in D.C., she met Dick — a Piedmont native — in North Carolina two years earlier. Dick lived there for six years, and she for nearly 10. They met while working for the same company. “We both worked for a ‘no-nonsense pantyhose’ company. She was in accounting, I in marketing,” Dick recalled. “We’d go to brunch a lot. That’s what we did before online dating.” After one more year in North Carolina, where Mary had attended college, the two spent nearly three years in St. Louis, where their daughter Katherine, was born in 1985. Now 37, she works for AT&T corporate headquarters in Dallas, Texas. “We’d planned to live in the D.C. area,” said Dick, “but we were both corporate gypsies. We always bonded over our love of traveling, and we’ve instilled the same in our children.” In 1986, the three returned to California to head four Wendy’s hamburger restaurant franchises in Mendocino County, living in Ukiah. Dick working seven days a week and Mary working six — taking one day off to care for Katherine. “Since our marriage survived the Wendy’s experience, it can survive anything,” said Mary wryly. In 1988, the Carters sold their “Wendy’s experience” and moved to Piedmont, Dick’s hometown. They have been here for 35 years this August. Dick returned to marketing, working first for a San Francisco agency and then for his alma mater, UC Berkeley. In 1992, the couple celebrated the birth of twin boys. I remember thinking before the Ultrasound, ‘It’s a good thing the kids will be so many years apart, so no two will be in college at the same time,” Mary said. “Famous last words; they were twins.” Michael and William are now 31. Michael lives in Oakland and works for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s after-school Schoolmates program. William works as the interim General Manager of Merrill Gardens at Rolling Hills Estates, a senior living home outside Torrance in Southern California. All three of the Carter kids grew up much like their father, who attended Havens Elementary School, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School. The Carter children attended Wildwood Elementary, where Mary began teaching as a paraeducator 20 years ago. “I was born in Seattle, so the kids tell me that they all graduated from Wildwood and I never did,” said Mary with a laugh. “Dick always loved Piedmont. Even when we were in North Carolina, he’d always be looking for Dick and Mary Carter in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile in 2016. a Bay Area-style brown shingle house for us.” Mary’s volunteer experience includes the Piedmont Neighbors & Newcomers Club the Piedmont High School Parent Club; the nonprofit Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy & Information in Special Education (of which she is a founding member); and Pack 5 and Troop 11 of the Piedmont Scouts. Dick is well-known in Piedmont as a longtime high school football coach, and more recently as a member of the city’s Recreation Commission, He co-founded and frequently leads the Walking on Wednesdays group since 2018,, and recently added a book group and movie group – primarily for seniors – to his arsenal of activities designed for Piedmonters. “Dick got the idea (of weekly walks) from me; I walked every block of Piedmont after work for over a decade, especially the hills. I was training to hike Mount Whitney,” Mary said. “In summer 2009, I finally did so with Mike and Will as part of their Eagle Scout work. I loved the views and the rich history the area held. Dick had the idea of having the Recreation Department sponsor Wednesday group and have it focus on local history,” she said. To celebrate their Valentine’s Day evening before today’s walk, Dick and Mary took a rare break from their outdoor activities and stayed home to share lobster ravioli over champagne. “Wine is one of our love languages,” confirmed Mary. “We’ve been particularly fond of Malbecs since travelling to Argentina and Chile over New Year’s in 2016.” “The holiday is about celebrating love in all its forms, after all,” said Mary. ”I’ve been so fortunate to have Dick in my life throughout the multiple chapters of our family. We hope for many more ahead.” “Yep. Let me add that Mary’s a great cook,” said Dick with a broad grin. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: On their first date, Frank and Michele Helm went to the movies. “He put his arm around my shoulders,” said Michele. “That was it, no creeping. I thought, wow, no moves for a fraternity boy – what’s wrong with this guy?” Afterward, he dropped her off at her sorority house. “We sat in my driveway and talked for three hours straight.” Frank, a man of relatively few words, contemplated this for a moment. “Maybe she talked for three hours and I listened, because I still vividly remember what she looked like — she had on this Brooks Brothers sweater.” “I still have the sweater,” Michele replied. The two met in February 1981 at the Kingfish Pub in North Oakland. Frank, then a senior at UC Berkeley, was bartending; Michele was ending her freshman year. With Frank about to leave for dental school in Boston, Michele decided to leave Berkeley and come with him. “He wanted me to keep him company on the drive (to the East Coast) and then fly back,” she said. “No way. I checked myself into the Y, he stayed with a rugby friend, I said ‘You want to do anything, you know where I am.’ Since I was the only other person he knew in town, he called. I worked as an administrative assistant while studying graphic design [at the Art Institute there.]” For many years Michele has been a highly skilled and in-demand graphic designer. After Frost spent four years at Boston University, the couple moved back to the Bay Area and lived in Chinatown and Pacific Heights in San Francisco. After three years of general practice, Frank returned to school for a two-year orthodontic residency program at the University of the Pacific. After his residency, Frank got a job offer at a practice on Grand Avenue on the Oakland-Piedmont border where he still works. The Helms were married on February 1, 1986, five years after they met. articles.text: Pouyan Assadi has been promoted as head coach of the track and field team. The Piedmont High track and field team will have a new face at the helm this spring. Running coach Jeanine Holmlund was informed in January that after 10 years on the job, her contract was not being renewed. Ironically her track and field team last year set a handful of new school records. The school’s sprint coach Pouyan Assadi is being named as the new track & field head coach. “I loved coaching the team and took a lot of extra time to try to make it fun for our athletes. We had both fun and success over my 10 years,” said Holmlund. “The team welcomed anyone who wanted to put in their best effort. Leaders worked for the team and remained humble despite their success. We have a good group of juniors and sophomores who have already taken on this holistic spirit. I told Bradley [Athletic Director Bradley Smet] in the fall that I thought Pouyan Assadi would make a good head coach some day while I was thinking about who would I trust to eventually take my place,” said Holmlund. Holmlund said the team should be in “good hands” with Assadi. “I’ve brought the track and field program a long way from when I started, and I also contributed time to the WACC league, so I’m happy to leave it in good hands with people I know and trust. I truly expect to see a few [more] school records broken and wish [to see] all our athletes reach their goals,” she added. The decision seemed be a shocking move for the school to after the historic 2022 season. Parker Terrill set the school’s pole vault record several times; Jack Stein became the 1600 and 3200 record holder; Ellie Black accomplished the school’s second and third all-time best times in the 1600 and 3200; and the 4x400 relay team of Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long broke a 30-year old school record. By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont High track and field team will have a new face at the helm this spring. Running coach Jeanine Holmlund was informed in January that after 10 years on the job, her contract was not being renewed. Ironically her track and field team last year set a handful of new school records. The school’s sprint coach Pouyan Assadi is being named as the new track & field head coach. “I loved coaching the team and took a lot of extra time to try to make it fun for our athletes. We had both fun and success over my 10 years,” said Holmlund. “The team welcomed anyone who wanted to put in their best effort. Leaders worked for the team and remained humble despite their success. We have a good group of juniors and sophomores who have already taken on this holistic spirit. I told Bradley [Athletic Director Bradley Smet] in the fall that I thought Pouyan Assadi would make a good head coach some day while I was thinking about who would I trust to eventually take my place,” said Holmlund. Holmlund said the team should be in “good hands” with Assadi. “I’ve brought the track and field program a long way from when I started, and I also contributed time to the WACC league, so I’m happy to leave it in good hands with people I know and trust. I truly expect to see a few [more] school records broken and wish [to see] all our athletes reach their goals,” she added. The decision seemed be a shocking move for the school to after the historic 2022 season. Parker Terrill set the school’s pole vault record several times; Jack Stein became the 1600 and 3200 record holder; Ellie Black accomplished the school’s second and third all-time best times in the 1600 and 3200; and the 4x400 relay team of Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long broke a 30-year old school record. articles.text: Highlands beat Mt. Eden, Castro Valley to close regular season Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team closed its season in a strong way, defeating Mt. Eden 3-1 on Tuesday, February 7 at Witter Field and upsetting Castro Valley 1-0 on the road on Friday, February 10. Piedmont ends its regular season with an 8-6-4 (W-T-L) overall record and 7-6-3 in league, to finish in 4th place. They closed the season on a three-match winning streak. “We played them (Castro Valley) the week before, so we felt like we knew how to match up against them. It was a tight game and we were able to score on a breakaway. It feels great to get some momentum going into NCS,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Piedmont enters the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 8 seed and is set to host No. 9 St. Helena tonight, Wednesday, February 15 at Witter Field in the first round of the post-season. “I would have liked a better seed, but that’s how it goes. We just have to accept that and be ready,” said coach Sullivan. ‘We don’t know much about St. Helena, but it should be pretty close. They’ve gotten some good results against the No. 3 seed, Roseland University Prep.” With a victory, Piedmont would likely travel to Santa Rosa to take on the No. 1 seed, Cardinal Newman, this Saturday, February 18. The Highlanders lost to the Cardinals 2-0 on January 6. PHS is the defending Division 4 NCS champions. 3-1 win over Mt. Eden The Highlanders led 1-0 by the end of the first half and the match was tied briefly in the second half before PHS tacked on two more goals. Prior to the game, Piedmont honored its 14 seniors on Senior Night: Brady Hinsch, Andrew Szerdy, Evan Manolis, Soren Dixon, Miles Corcoran, T.J. O’Neil, William Daniel, Myles Gray, Owen Grippando, Jack Nelson, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Max Schleuning, Jordan Miller, and goalie Daniel Malecki. Piedmont’s first goal came in the 20th minute by Evan Manolis following a long throw-in by Jack Nelson. The long toss bounced around the top of the penalty area after Mt. Eden failed to clear the ball. Manolis dashed in front of the Monarchs’ defender for the volley and looped the ball into the net. Mt. Eden tied the game in the 50th minute, but Piedmont regained the lead in the 67th on a corner kick when the ball trickled in front of the net until falling to Woolwine, who finished it off. articles.text: PHS girls earn No. 3 seed in NCS playoffs; play Sacred Heart tonight Photos by Todd Marshburn PHS honored its 10 seniors on the roster. In a successful end to the regular season, Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team won its final three games, capped by a huge 1-nil upset of this year’s Western Alameda County Conference champions, Berkeley, on Wednesday, February 8. The Highlanders finished second in league with a 7-1-4 record (9-1-5 overall), four points shy of the Yellowjackets, who have now won five consecutive league titles. PHS honored its 10 members of the Class of 2023 on Senior Night on Wednesday: Morgan Hunt, Michaela Bini, Ellie DeVan, Kyra Dang, Audrey Harmon, Sophie Hebert, Emily Fitzgerald, Siena Riddel, Audrey Lam, and Cameron Lorin. articles.text: PHS senior Heather Stoneman (right) led a group of over 30 female mountain bike riders for the Girls Riding Together (GRiT) event at Joaquin Miller. A light drizzle on Saturday, February 11, did not deter Girls Riding Together (GRiT) as 35 girls, women coaches, and moms from Piedmont and Oakland joined together to ride their mountain bikes in the dirt, work on skills and have fun. Attendees had a wide range of ages from middle school to high school from several schools in the East Bay. Heather Stoneman, co-captain of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team and a senior at Piedmont High, led the event and gathered girls from all riding levels at Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills. Stoneman was chosen by the NorcCal league as a GRiT Ambassador this year. Her role involves encouraging more girls to try Mountain Biking and host GRiT rides. In addition, she worked to bring in adult coaches from different East Bay mountain bike teams to put on the event. “That was so much fun. I loved seeing all of those girls out on the trails!” said Katrina Rapa, Oakland DEVO coach. FUTURE EVENTS The PHS Mountain Bike team will have its first race of the season this Saturday, February 18, in Modesto. The Piedmont DEVO team will compete the following day, Sunday, February 19. The PHS team is currently running an “Everest Challenge” fundraiser in which riders are challenged to ride 29,000 feet in the month of February. Community members are encouraged to support them by pledging online at: www.pledgeit.org/phs-mtb-everest-challenge. Piedmont DEVO, the team at Piedmont Middle School, is still accepting new riders, both girls and boys. To learn more and sign up, go to: https://piedmontdevo. com/. articles.text: Have you ever seen a group of kids asking for more vegetables? At Fairyland’s Summer Day Camp that actually happened. Campers who joined our Farm to Table session eagerly asked for seconds of carrots and celery after making and tasting Green Goddess dressing. Farm to Table is one of two new camps Fairyland introduced last summer. In Farm to Table campers learn about gardening, animal husbandry, and the journey of how seeds become salads. Our camp area is transformed into an outdoor kitchen with the hustle and bustle of little chefs. Campers make mozzarella cheese, fresh pasta from scratch, and pickle some veggies. From getting their hands dirty, to feeling the joy of cooking, to anticipating that first taste of the fruit of their labor, the children are abuzz with excitement. The Farm to Table camp is two weeks of building practical life skills, making friends, and learning how to collaborate. The other new camp is Fairyland Puppeteer, which involves creating a puppet show from scratch and presenting a beautifully crafted performance to a live audience. Campers collaborate to devise a familiar story, design a puppet stage, make their own sock puppets, and learn how to act out their characters. articles.text: SF Jazz will host French jazz vocalist Cryille Aimee this weekend, February 18 and 19, at the Miner Auditorium in San Francisco. Aimee’s musical influences come from her French and Dominican background. She was raised in the northern French town of Samois-sur-Seine, the last home of jazz luminary Django Reinhardt. Aimée’s music is heavily influenced by Reinhardt and blends instrumentals from the gypsy lifestyle of Europe. articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora’s (MoAD) exhibition “The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion” is on view until March 5. The exhibit is in its West Coast premiere at MoAD in San Francusci and highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and beyond. Each artist’s work offers a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The exhibit has been curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard.

articles.text: Fashion historian Dr. Minjee Kim is guest lecturer On February 25, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum will host guest lecturer and fashion historian Dr. Minjee Kim, who will discuss eight exhibitions of Korean dress and fashion of the last decade. Kim is a full-time professor at Jeonju Kijeon College and holds adjunct positions at Seoul National University in South Korea, and Academy of Art University in San Francisco. She has served on the board of the Costume Society of America since 2018, and joined Tracing Patterns Foundation as a research associate in 2022. In this one-day lecture and exhibition, Kim will describe the growing international influence of Korean popular trends in fashion in the Western world. The presentation will provide an overview of Korean fashion and its history, both through a classical and modern lens. The event is available both in person and online via Zoom. Registration is required at https:// www.famsf.org/events/fashion-museology-korean-fashion-exhibitions. An exhibit titled Korean Fashion: From Royal Court to Runway is now on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.

articles.text: Opera review by Paul Hertelendy Doubts abounded, with nay-sayers smirking that not even Verdi could set a Shakespearean comedy into a good opera. Those doubting Thomases were silenced when nearing the then-doddering age of 80, Verdi brought off that sparkling operatic masterpiece, Falstaff, which is getting its due and more from a highly animated production at Opera San José. Major companies take note: This smaller troupe with its actor-singers, and only in its 38th season, can run circles around many grand-opera troupes having major funding and backing. The production that opened February 11 struck the delicate balance, with ample buffoonish humor, but without turning the obese, aged knight into a buffoon. However much his earthy desires were thwarted, Falstaff shook off his dunking in the Thames and maintained a measure of self-worth. He walked that tightrope, laughing off the pranks he underwent with the deft final fugue, “All the World Is Mirth.” Baritone Darren Lekeith Drone walks that precarious tightrope, winebelly and all, and sings with sensual ease, however preposterous. Falstaff sings a paean to wine – how appropriate to us Californians! He is surrounded by similar barflies. And the opera’s main setting is inside a giant wine barrel, even bigger than the famous Falstaff belly that surpasses even the one-time mighty frame of Luciano Pavarotti. The production under Stage Director José Maria Condemi then sets in motion a seamless comedy with glints of Shakespeare’s England, and supertitle translations in both English and Spanish. Among the men, the robust baritone Eugene Brancoveanu plays the tricky role of Ford as if anticipating General Motors soon to appear in pursuit. Unforgettable is the interplay of him and Falstaff, as the knight reaches repeatedly toward the money-sack offered, in time to the music, till he succumbs and grabs it. This troupe has moved forward on many fronts to produce a great show with its elusive challenge now lighting up San Jose; it’s only a matter of time till the struggling pit orchestra follows suit. OSJ continues its long tradition of featuring a rotating complement of resident artists, no less than five of them appearing in Falstaff. Opera San Jose Notes A sub-rosa compliment was paid to the company when its general director Khori Dastoor was tapped by the mighty Houston Grand Opera to take over leadership. The OSJ successor starting in 2022 has been Shawna Lucey. The three-act opera ran just two-and-a-half hours with the elimination of the other intermission. Reducing the endless intermissions to tighten up the action has been a crusade in some opera circles, voiced loudly and often by San Francisco Opera sage and philanthropist Gordon Getty. February 9 marked exactly 130 years since the world premiere of the opera. Verdi’s Opera Falstaff, in Italian, through Feb. 26. For info: (408) 437-4450, or online: boxoffice@operasj.org. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s production of The Headlands is currently being performed in the Toni Rembe theatre in San Francisco through March 5. The Headlands is Obie Award-winning playwright Christopher Chen’s newest play, described as “a complicated love letter” to San Francisco. The play tells the story of true crime fan Henry Wong, whose father’s unexplained death is the ultimate cold case. Protagonist Wong digs into the San Francisco police department evidence, but he’s haunted by the past of his own family history and upbringing. “I am thrilled beyond measure to be bringing The Headlands to A.C.T., and to be working with Pam MacKinnon to bring it to life,” said Chen. “The Headlands is my love letter to San Francisco, the city I spent my entire life in, from birth up to right now. To share this play with my hometown, a place I feel so deeply in my bones, will be one of the most personally meaningful moments of my career,” To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/the-headlands/. Hatching plots and pranks is the quartet of Elizabethan ladies capped by the habile lyric soprano Chanáe Curtis playing Alice, supported by mezzo Shanley Horvitz (Meg), contralto Megan Esther Grey (Dame Quickly), and soprano Natalia Santaliz (the highly eligible Nannetta). The one thoroughly British scene, with nymphs in a bewitched forest, is capped by Santaliz’s fetching aria, before all the goblins materialize. articles.text: Guests attending a screening of Harold and Maude at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. When a 17-year-old boy’s mother gives him a sports car, he fires up his blowtorch and converts it into a hearse. That’s just one quirky moment in the 1971 movie Harold and Maude, now considered a cult classic. Its screening drew an approving crowd of 20 viewers to the second gathering of Piedmont’s new movie group, the Second Thursday Flix Fest on February 9. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the movie group now takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. It meets on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. Participants are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. Darby Gragg gave a detailed introduction to the film, which was directed by Hal Ashby. That blowtorch-wielding kid, Harold (Bud Cort) is troubled in a bizarre, charming way – we can’t help liking him. His odd psyche compels him to stage fake suicides, and the movie opens with one of them, in which he pretends to hang himself. His audience of choice is his mother, played by an amusingly arch Vivian Pickles. Wise to his tricks, she’s never alarmed – she just wants to get him married and out of the house. Harold also likes to hang out at funerals, and that’s where Maude, a 79-year old pixie who is as unorthodox as he is, spots him and whisks him away in a stolen car. She lives in an abandoned railway wagon by the side of the road, and that’s where, as their relationship develops, she teaches him the banjo, bolsters him with affection, and, well, seduces him. Talk about May/December! Maude is played by the wonderful Ruth Gordon, and she and Bud Cort work well together in inhabiting a tale that is offbeat in the extreme but also often very funny. It’s a lighthearted black comedy that’s given extra fizz by several Cat Stevens songs. The Piedmont audience gave the film 100% thumbs up. Some comments were: “It’s a refreshing delight,” and, “It has lot of depth.” One viewer wondered “how young people would react to it,” and another liked how it advocated “accepting differences.” “Great music,” said another. The Second Thursday Flix Fest meets again on March 9 to view the Alfred Hitchcock classic thriller, North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant, Eva Marie Saint and James Mason. There is now space for more people to attend. The group is open to anyone over 18 years of age, and there are no fees. Participants may attend on a drop-in basis with no obligations. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at: https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Robert Hall is the longtime theater and dance reviewer in the Piedmont Post.

pages.text: Wednesday, February 15, 2023 23 New Piedmont movie group views a cult classic Guests attending a screening of Harold and Maude at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. By Bob Hall When a 17-year-old boy’s mother gives him a sports car, he fires up his blowtorch and converts it into a hearse. That’s just one quirky moment in the 1971 movie Harold and Maude, now considered a cult classic. Its screening drew an approving crowd of 20 viewers to the second gathering of Piedmont’s new movie group, the Second Thursday Flix Fest on February 9. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the movie group now takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. It meets on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. Participants are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. Darby Gragg gave a detailed introduction to the film, which was directed by Hal Ashby. That blowtorch-wielding kid, Harold (Bud Cort) is troubled in a bizarre, charming way – we can’t help liking him. His odd psyche compels him to stage fake suicides, and the movie opens with one of them, in which he pretends to hang himself. His audience of choice is his mother, played by an amusingly arch Vivian Pickles. Wise to his tricks, she’s never alarmed – she just wants to get him married and out of the house. Harold also likes to hang out at funerals, and that’s where Maude, a 79-year old pixie who is as unorthodox as he is, spots him and whisks him away in a stolen car. She lives in an abandoned railway wagon by the side of the road, and that’s where, as their relationship develops, she teaches him the banjo, bolsters him with affection, and, well, seduces him. Talk about May/December! Maude is played by the wonderful Ruth Gordon, and she and Bud Cort work well together in inhabiting a tale that is offbeat in the extreme but also often very funny. It’s a lighthearted black comedy that’s given extra fizz by several Cat Stevens songs. The Piedmont audience gave the film 100% thumbs up. Some comments were: “It’s a refreshing delight,” and, “It has lot of depth.” One viewer wondered “how young people would react to it,” and another liked how it advocated “accepting differences.” “Great music,” said another. The Second Thursday Flix Fest meets again on March 9 to view the Alfred Hitchcock classic thriller, North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant, Eva Marie Saint and James Mason. There is now space for more people to attend. The group is open to anyone over 18 years of age, and there are no fees. Participants may attend on a drop-in basis with no obligations. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at: https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Robert Hall is the longtime theater and dance reviewer in the Piedmont Post. articles.text: Connie Herrick (front) of Piedmont Connect with the PHS Green Team. Piedmont High School (PHS) is about to become a garden oasis for bees and other pollinators. The PHS Green Club recently launched the “Bee-Friendly Flower Project,” an ambitious plan to install bee-friendly plants in concrete-lined boxes that extend along the walls and walkways of the library and the student center. This landscaping improvement is a much-needed bonus as these boxes are currently occupied by weeds or dead plants. “The planting will start in mid-Spring. We’re getting advice on what to plant from District Facilities Director Pete Palmer, and my mom, Gillian Atchley, who is a native plant gardener. We’ll put in a mix of native flowers that are low maintenance and low-water use,” said Green Club Co-President Max Rivera. The school district is providing the project’s infrastructure. “Possibly starting in the next few weeks, we’ll remove the old landscaping, add new soil amendment and install new irrigation where it’s needed. It’s a great environmental project,” said Palmer. The Green Club currently consists of 45 students and has 20 active members, who meet every week to discuss projects and potential volunteer activities, both within and outside Piedmont. They are supported by PHS history teacher David Keller, who has been the Green Club’s faculty advisor for the past decade. “These students are doing an amazing job for the campus,” he said. “They’re motivated and taking the initiative. I just try to get out of their way.” In addition to the bee-friendly boxes, the club supports the Climate Literacy Resolution, which advocates teaching California students from K-12 about climate change in every classroom. According to Schools for Climate Action, more than 40 California school districts and county education offices have already adopted the resolution. The club is trying to persuade the Piedmont School District to include it in the curriculum. Two years ago, Green Club Co-President Elena Blanco worked on the Club’s fundraising effort to install solar panels on the new high school. “We raised $60,000,” she said. The funds went toward installing solar panels on the mansard roof of the new classroom building, which Palmer noted, was a very difficult job and was greatly benefited with the club’s contribution. Club members also volunteer at city events, including recycling trash at the Harvest Festival and helping load compost at the city’s compost giveaways. Outside of Piedmont, Blanco and other club members volunteer at the Friends of Sausal Creek Nursery and seek out other local organizations to help. Asked what inspired her to get involved, Blanco said, “I wasn’t into hiking and the outdoors until I went backpacking with my aunt in Alaska. That opened my eyes to the beauty and joys of the outdoor world.” Rivera added, “I’ve been surrounded by nature all my life and (now) spend lots of time outdoors – on the mountain biking team, and rafting, rock climbing and hiking in Colorado. I feel like I should give back to nature.” As they walked around the front of the new high school building, Rivera and Blanco noted the scraggly, dying vines attached to vertical posts. “Here’s another opportunity for bee-friendly plants,” they said. The Green Club has a fundraising effort underway with the goal of raising $700 for the new pollinator plants, soil and irrigation. Piedmont Connect has issued a $350 matching grant to the Club to help launch the Bee-Friendly Pollinator Project. Donations may be made at: Gofundme.com/f/help-to-fundphs-green-club. articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met with a record turnout of 22 readers on February 6 at the Community Hall to discuss Prisoners of Geography, a 2015 non-fiction book about geopolitics by British author and journalist Tim Marshall. The group included Bob and Mady Hall, Mike and Nancy Henn, Melba Yee, Richard Sigel, Carol Warren, Martin Levy, Gerry and Darby Gragg, Ken Young, Lisa Euphrat, Leigh Sorensen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lois Price, Laura Goldman, Adrienne Hamlin, Karin Fetherston, Susan Ode, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. In the book, Marshall uses 10 maps of regions around the world to explain the geopolitical situations and strategies of world powers. Marshall explains that all leaders of nations are constrained by geography. Their choices are limited by mountains, rivers, and seas. Writers often focus on people, ideas, and political movements, but without geography we never fully understand world events. The author explains that Russia lacks its own warm-water ports. Some of its Arctic ports freeze each winter, and Russian ships must contend with the ice packs to the north of the Arctic coastline. Additionally, the flat plain on Russia’s western border provides an easy route for invaders. Marshal contends these needs and conditions made Russia’s annexation of Crimea inevitable. His chapter on Russia, written in 2015, seems prophetic in the light of its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Prisoners of Geography was another great book for a discussion. Some loved it while others didn’t care for it, so the book provided a catalyst for related topic conversations. Those on the positive side felt they learned a lot, but many readers didn’t understand how geography can affect populations and cultures. They learned how mountains and rivers can keep people from interacting. This was as much a book on history as geography. Readers said Marshall’s detailed information was helpful, and they would now look at maps differently. They said it helped them better understand Putin’s motivations for invading Ukraine. They liked Marshall’s easy writing style and occasion humor too. Those on the negative side they felt the book overpromised and the title was misleading. Ten maps didn’t explain everything about the world, and the book didn’t provide an understanding of different people’s humanity, or how technology will affect the limiting effects of geography. The book generated some side discussions about the relative strengths of the American and Chinese cultural structures. Members of the group also shared experiences in countries where geographic barriers and language dialects can keep people from understanding one another. With their discussion complete the group considered their next books. They had previously selected The Buddha in the Attic, a 2011 novel by American author Julie Otsuka, for March, and Trevor Noah’s memoir, Born a Crime, as the April selection. The group’s next discussion will be on March 6 at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting, they will meet outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4.

articles.text: Robert (Bob) Ball, a native Piedmonter and in recent years a resident of Pleasant Hill, passed away of neck cancer at his home on February 6, 2023. He was surrounded his family and died 20 days shy of his 77th birthday. Born on February 26, 1946, in Wisconsin, Bob moved with his family to Piedmont at the age of six. He went through the Piedmont public schools, where he was a star athlete in track and football and earned the coveted Kurkjian Award in football as a junior and senior. The award is given to the athlete who demonstrates the ideals of sportsmanship and team play. While in high school he served as both captain of the football team and student body president. He graduated from Piedmont High in 1964, and then from San Jose State University. He later received his master’s degree in hospital administration from U.C. Berkeley. In his early career, he focused on rural health care in California while working at Woodland Memorial Hospital. After moving back to Piedmont in 1985, he went into hospital administration at the Surgery Center in Oakland and ended his career in 2010 with an anesthesiologist group in Walnut Creek. Bob loved having fun and knew how to have a good time. He loved being outdoors, whether camping, hiking, gardening, or water sports. In the 1980s-1990s, he spent many happy summers on family camping trips to Shaver Lake and Bernie Falls waterskiing, boogie boarding, and playing Bob Ball with his beloved 1970 GTO rounds of Pit, Canasta, and Jenkins Says. He became the stuff of legends in his family. In his retirement, Bob enjoyed traveling, first internationally, and more recently, throughout the Southwest of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. At home, he spent his leisure time tending his roses and building an impressive world for his Lionel model trains. Throughout his life, Bob was devoted to Piedmont and his close friends from elementary and high school. He played a central role in organizing his class of 1964 reunions and annual gatherings and proudly drove his blue 1970 GTO in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade over the years. Bob is survived by his partner, Lynne Deutscher, and his four children and their spouses: Jeremy Ball and wife Amy, Jeffrey Ball and wife Maggie, Joe Ball, Bob Ball, an avid water skier, in 1984 Bob Ball holds the football team’s coveted Kurkjian Award, which he won as a junior and senior at Piedmont High School. and Jordan Tharp and husband Kevin; his six grandchildren: Charlie, Julia, Emily, Benjamin, Ellie, and Nolan. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations in Bob’s honor be made to the American Cancer Society or the League to Save Lake Tahoe. The family hopes his friends honor Bob by listening to his favorite music, the Beach Boys, and enjoying time outdoors. The family will hold a celebration of Bob’s life at a later date. articles.text: The Piedmont Ladies Tennis Club (PLTC) recently donated $1700 to the Piedmont Recreation Department. According to PLTC President Beth Hurwich, the funds will go toward maintenance of tennis courts used by the club, including a new net at the courts on Vista Avenue. PLTC has a proud history of investment in the Piedmont community, with donations of more than $15,000 to the Recreation Department over the past 15 years. PLTC was a “Silver” donor at $4000 for the Hampton Court renovation, and contributed $2500 to the Corey Reich Tennis Center. Tennis loving women from Piedmont and the surrounding area are welcome to join PLTC. Intermediate and advanced players meet as the A-Ladder group on Tuesday mornings from 8:30 to 10 a.m. Beginner and intermediate players meet as the B-Ladder group from 9:00 to 10:30 a.m. on Wednesdays. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2023 Two Decades of Data Our residential real estate market has undergone dramatic changes over the past couple of decades. Looking back at 20 years of sales in Piedmont, we found several interesting stories in the data. First, while we saw variation in appreciation rates over time, primarily due to the “Great Recession,” Piedmont still performed well. Homes appreciated 5% per year, on average, over the last two decades. Second, the highest number of sales on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) for Piedmont was 153 in 2002, likely accompanying the recovery from the “dot-com bust” in 2000. Not surprisingly, the lowest number of total sales was 75 in 2008. The next highest number of sales was 148 in 2021, likely a combination of a low interest rate environment and households electing to make different lifestyle decisions as a result of Covid-19.
